hints: Focus on what must be present for conduction, free moving charged ions, and how this differs in a melt versus in water.
Notice that Y conducts even as a pure liquid, so it must already contain mobile ions when molten, which points to an ionic lattice.
Consider why Z is non-conducting when pure but conducting in water, think of a covalent chloride that reacts with water to release ions.
walkthrough:
**What makes a liquid conduct?**

Think side by side with me. Conduction needs mobile charged particles. In a molten ionic compound the lattice breaks down and ions can move, so it conducts well.

Rule to remember:
$$\text{molten ionic = mobile ions = conducts, molten covalent = neutral molecules = does not conduct}$$

**Identify Y**

Y conducts well both as a liquid and when added to water. That is classic ionic behaviour. It melts to give mobile ions, and it dissolves in water to give hydrated mobile ions.

$$\text{Y = ionic compound, soluble in water}$$

**Identify Z**

Z does not conduct as a pure liquid, so it cannot be ionic. It must be covalent with neutral molecules. But when added to water it does conduct, so it must react with water to form ions.

$$\text{Z = covalent compound that hydrolyses in water to give } \text{H}^+ \text{ and anions}$$

**Match to the formulae**

$\text{NaF}$ is ionic and very soluble, so it fits Y perfectly. $\text{SiCl}_4$ is covalent tetrahedral, non-conducting as a liquid, but it hydrolyses fully:
$$\text{SiCl}_4 + 4\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{Si(OH)}_4 + 4\text{HCl}$$
The $\text{HCl}$ formed ionises completely to give mobile $\text{H}^+$ and $\text{Cl}^-$ ions, so the mixture conducts well. $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$ is ionic but insoluble in water, so it cannot give a conducting aqueous mixture.

options.A: Incorrect. $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$ as Y is wrong because although molten $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$ conducts, it is insoluble in water and does not give a conducting aqueous mixture.
options.B: Incorrect. $\text{NaF}$ is correct for Y, but $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$ cannot be Z. Z must be non-conducting as a liquid but conducting in water, while $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$ is insoluble and gives no ions in water.
options.C: Correct. Y is $\text{NaF}$, an ionic solid that gives mobile $\text{Na}^+$ and $\text{F}^-$ ions both when molten and when dissolved. Z is $\text{SiCl}_4$, a covalent liquid with no mobile ions, but it hydrolyses in water to produce $\text{H}^+$ and $\text{Cl}^-$ ions which conduct well.
options.D: Incorrect. This reverses the logic. $\text{SiCl}_4$ cannot be Y because as a covalent liquid it has no mobile ions and does not conduct. $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$ cannot be Z because it does not dissolve to give a conducting solution.
